content:
Starting this thread to ask some questions about MathEconLib announced here: #Project announcements > MathEconLib

  1. What is the status of AI assistance with respect to contributions? Is it allowed? Are there any aspects of AI assisted work that the maintainers would like human operators to check in particular?
  2. I'm interested in the concept of Price of Anarchy in congested networks. Is there anything on that in the library? If not, where would it go?

Thanks @Bolton Bailey, great questions.

  1. Regarding AI, check out the note on our website. In short: It's not a pure autoformalization project. Definitions and conventions are developed by economic theorists for consistency with our design principles. However, we welcome researchers to use AI to help with formalization and proof development. 1. Contributions receive human review, particularly to ensure that definitions, assumptions, and theorem statements faithfully capture the intended economics.
  2. Price of anarchy in networks is definitely the type of application we'd like to support. We don't currently have the network layer built. I'd imagine a general price-of-anarchy abstraction building on our game-theory foundations, with congestion networks as a specialized application. It's definitely within scope, but we haven't yet built out those layers. If you're interested in helping develop this, feel free to DM!

I'm a bit sad to see it is targeting a 7 month old toolchain. Could that be updated? I think it's important for libraries to have a credible maintenance story, and updating to recent toolchains/Mathlib versions is a first step towards that.

A large fraction of the library is in the file https://github.com/matheconlib/matheconlib/blob/main/MathEconLib/ForMathlib/Schauder.lean#L18, which says

This file is the original auto-formalisation output (see the module doc below) and has not been through the library's review discipline.

It also turns off quite a few of the linters.
There's no CI check that would guard against the use of sorry or an axiom, so the project is hard to audit.

And my AIs immediately claim that there is an incorrect definition:

:robot: says

The definition of Auction.BIC is wrong when bidders’ values are correlated: it averages over opponents’ values without conditioning on the bidder’s own value.

For example, let two bidders have values (0,0) or (1,1), each with probability 1/2. Allocate nothing and charge each bidder (2b₁-1)(2b₂-1), where b₁,b₂ are their reports. For every fixed report, the library computes an expected payment of zero, so Auction.BIC holds. But either bidder knows the other’s value from their own: reporting truthfully costs 1, while reporting the opposite value earns 1.

The same example makes expectedRevenue return 0, although actual revenue under truthful reporting is always 2.

These definitions need independence assumptions or expectations conditional on the bidder’s own value. The symmetric-IPV revenue-equivalence theorem already assumes independence and is not refuted by this example.

See https://gist.github.com/kim-em/029ff60dda65a86eaceea73561967599

(To be clear, I am not a mathematical economist, and make no particular claim about this criticism, but you might want to take it to a mathematical economist!)
Thanks, Kim. I appreciate you taking the time to look through this. I'll look into each of these points and follow up shortly.

Thanks Kim. The definition your AI flagged is a real bug: our BIC ignored correlation between bidders’ values. Bo has a counterexample and a fix up at matheconlib/matheconlib#210. On the toolchain, the bump to v4.35.0 is up and building green at matheconlib/matheconlib#220, and matheconlib/matheconlib#209 tracks the rest of your points.

I'll just point out the finding this bug only required:

Hey Sol or Opus, please find a significant error in this library.

... generally worth doing this oneself these days!

Agreed, and that prompt had already been running: a referee pass over current main finished this morning and is being folded into matheconlib/matheconlib#209, alongside Bo's own audit. The sorry/axiom check is in CI now. One lesson already: a single pass misses things an outside reader catches, so we are running more than one and cross-checking rather than trusting any one of them.
